newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S., Mexico in show of unity before Clinton trip.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico in show of unity before Clinton trip.

text.p: U.S. and Mexican officials scrambled to praise each other's governments before President Bill Clinton's first visit to Mexico next week, but political analysts said the show of unity masked differences on key issues and a lack of real enthusiasm among Mexicans.

The May 5-7 trip comes at a difficult time for relations between Washington and its southern neighbor, strained this year by tough new U.S. measures against illegal immigration and a series of embarrassing drug scandals in Mexico.

The crackdown on migration caused alarm in Mexico -- the biggest source of migrants to the United States -- and the spat over drugs caused deep resentment because many Mexicans believe the narcotics problem is the result of American demand rather than Latin supply.

Attempting to smooth Clinton's path, White House special envoy Thomas McLarty said here on April 21 that cooperation between Washington and Mexico was "at an all-time high" and played down controversial topics.
U.S. Ambassador James Jones told local reporters this week that relations were "the best I've seen in general terms" and predicted that Clinton's visit would have an "enormously positive effect."

President Ernesto Zedillo, addressing a forum in Atlanta on Tuesday, hailed Clinton as a "statesman of great vision and character" and praised the "respect and solidarity" he had shown for Mexico at difficult moments.
Mexican political analysts, while recognizing the generally warm personal relations between Clinton and the Yale-educated Zedillo, were less euphoric.

"It's not the best time for Clinton to visit," Lorenzo Meyer, a political scientist at the Colegio de Mexico, told Reuters. "We have a pretty unpleasant climate of mutual accusations (over drugs) ... I don't think Mexican public opinion will have much enthusiasm for receiving Clinton."

Reflecting sensitivity on the Mexican side, a spokeswoman for the attorney general's office told Reuters all interviews for foreign correspondents with Mexican drug officials were on hold until after the Clinton visit.

Zedillo aides hope the Mexican public will remember Clinton's role in securing the $13.5 billion U.S. rescue package that helped lift Mexico out of economic crisis in 1995 and his leadership in winning congressional approval of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) in 1993.
They also gratefully recall how the Clinton administration mobilized allies in Congress in March to fight off a proposal to deny Mexico recognition as a drug war ally and cut off aid.
"The U.S. government has always understood us," purred a senior Zedillo administration member. "The complications we have had came from below government level."

Underlining the close coordination between Washington and Mexico City to guarantee the trip's success, Mexico announced on Wednesday the creation of a new anti-drug agency to replace its National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD).

Officials said they recognized that the INCD had become hopelessly corrupt and discredited in its four years of existence and promised that the new body would recruit only honest, well-trained, well-rewarded special agents.
The White House applauded the decision on Thursday as a "positive and encouraging development taken independently by the government of Mexico."

But Mexican commentators were already noting that the new Special Prosecutor's Office for Crimes Against Health was the latest in a series of special organizations set up to fight drugs, none of which has achieved any lasting success.

"How long will this (new organization) last ?" asked Reforma newspaper. "It's worth asking because entities are created to fight drug trafficking and then disappear all the time. ... Will it be different now ?"
